_about: The weekly mysteries (game/core/weekly_mystery.gd): five clues, one opening each weekday, one guess.

mysteries.title: The monsoon fever
mysteries.patient: Mr. Santosh Kadam, 34, office peon, Kurla
clues: Fever, headache and a body ache 'like a truck went over me', five days now. Paracetamol from the chemist, twice.
His calves hurt so much he can't climb the stairs at the station. He says it's the calves, specifically. He's very specific.
Last Tuesday the trains stopped and he waded home through knee-deep flood water. 'Everyone did, Doctor. What to do?'
His eyes are red, but there's no discharge and nothing itches. His urine has gone dark and there's not much of it. Creatinine 3.1.
Today he's yellow. Platelets 62,000, bilirubin 6. The rat poison shop near his chawl is doing very good business.
mysteries.explain: Flood water, rats, terrible calf pain, red eyes without discharge, then kidneys and jaundice: leptospirosis. Every Mumbai monsoon. Doxycycline or penicillin, and dialysis if the kidneys stop.

mysteries.title: The farmer who kept coming back
clues: Fever for eight days, high, with chills. Malaria test negative twice. Typhoid test 'weakly positive', which means nothing.
Bad headache, a dry cough, and his eyes are a bit red. Two courses of antibiotics from the village clinic did nothing.
Lymph nodes swollen in the armpit. Liver enzymes up, platelets 90,000.
Before the fever, he spent a week clearing scrub and long grass on the bund behind his field.
Under his left arm, where nobody looked: a painless black scab with a red ring round it, like a cigarette burn.
mysteries.explain: Fever that ignores ordinary antibiotics, bush clearing, and an eschar hiding in the armpit: scrub typhus, from a mite bite. Doxycycline works in a day or two. Always look in the armpits and the groin.

mysteries.title: The battery man's stomach
clues: Belly cramps on and off for two months, bad enough to bend him double. Two scans: nothing. 'Gas,' said the last doctor.
Constipated, tired, and his haemoglobin is 9. Iron tablets for a month have changed nothing.
His right wrist has gone weak; he can't lift his hand back. He keeps dropping his chai glass.
He works in a small battery recycling unit. No gloves, no mask, and lunch on the workbench.
A thin blue-grey line along his gums. The blood film shows red cells with little dots in them (basophilic stippling).
mysteries.explain: Colicky belly pain, anaemia that iron doesn't fix, wrist drop, a gum line and stippled red cells, in a battery recycler: lead. Blood lead level, out of the exposure, and chelation if it's high.

mysteries.title: The tingling feet
clues: Her feet tingle and burn, worse at night. She's been told it's 'just age'. She disagrees, strongly.
She's tired all the time, a bit breathless on the stairs, and pale. Her tongue is red, smooth and sore.
Strictly vegetarian all her life, no eggs. Diabetic for twelve years, on metformin the whole time.
Haemoglobin 9.2, but the red cells are big: MCV 112. Iron studies normal.
She's become forgetful, and in the dark she sways when she closes her eyes. Her daughter thought it was the start of dementia.
mysteries.explain: Big red cells, a sore tongue, tingling, unsteadiness in the dark and forgetfulness, in a lifelong vegetarian on metformin: B12 deficiency. Injections fix it, if it's caught before the nerves give up.

mysteries.title: Tired, cold and gaining
clues: Exhausted for six months. She sleeps nine hours and wakes up tired. Her husband says she's 'just lazy now'.
Five kilos up without eating more. Constipated. She wears a sweater in May, in Nagpur.
Her skin is dry, her hair is falling out, and her periods have become heavy.
Her voice is hoarse, her face looks puffy in the mornings, and her pulse is 54.
Her ankle reflexes come back slowly, like they're thinking about it. Cholesterol has gone up too.
mysteries.explain: Tired, cold, weight up, constipated, dry skin, heavy periods, a slow pulse and slow reflexes: an underactive thyroid. A TSH test and a tablet a day. Somebody should also have a word with the husband.

mysteries.title: The back that wouldn't get better
clues: Back pain for three months, in the middle of the back. Physiotherapy and painkillers: no change.
The pain wakes him at night. He's lost six kilos and doesn't feel like eating.
A low fever every evening, and sweats that soak the sheet. His roommate had a cough 'for a long time' last year.
Pressing on one bone in the middle of his back makes him jump. A small bump is starting to stick out there.
The X-ray shows two vertebrae collapsing into each other, and the disc between them is gone.
mysteries.explain: Months of back pain with night pain, weight loss, evening fevers and sweats, a contact with a cough, and two vertebrae eaten away with the disc: TB of the spine (Pott's). Six months or more of TB treatment, free under the national programme.

mysteries.title: The boy who stopped growing
clues: Short for his age, and smaller than his younger cousin. His mother says he 'eats like a horse'.
Loose, pale, smelly stools, and a big belly on thin arms and legs.
Anaemic. A year of iron syrup hasn't helped at all.
It all started at about one year old, around when his grandmother began giving him chapatis.
A blood test for tissue transglutaminase antibodies comes back strongly positive.
mysteries.explain: Poor growth, pale fatty stools, a big belly, anaemia that iron can't fix, all starting with wheat: coeliac disease. Common in North India. No wheat, ever, and he catches up.

mysteries.title: The anaemia that iron didn't fix
clues: Her haemoglobin is 10.4. The college doctor started iron tablets. A year later: 10.5.
She feels fine. She's never had heavy periods, and she eats well (her hostel mess disagrees).
The red cells are very small: MCV 63. But her red cell count is high, 6.1 million.
Her ferritin is normal. So is her serum iron.
HbA2 on electrophoresis: 5.6%. Her parents are first cousins, and her mother 'has also been anaemic forever'.
mysteries.explain: Very small cells with a high red cell count, normal iron and a raised HbA2: beta thalassaemia trait. Stop the iron. And test the partner before marriage, because two traits can make a child with thalassaemia major.
